title: Social Media's Initial Reaction to Information and Misinformation on Ebola, August 2014: Facts and Rumors
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of Ebola-related microblog posts on Twitter (1% random firehose sample filtered on the keyword 'Ebola') and Sina Weibo (search-engine retrieval of two Chinese Ebola terms), in two 24-hour windows around the WHO PHEIC announcement of 8 August 2014. Random ~6% subsamples were manually coded into content categories including 'alternative health information' (information not in line with current scientific understanding of Ebola), giving shares of items that were misinformation with explicit denominators (Table 3).

estimates.country: No geographical restriction on the sample (English-language tweets only)
estimates.date: Batch 1: August 8, 2014 06:50:00 GMT to August 9, 2014 06:49:59 GMT (the 24 hours after the WHO PHEIC announcement)
estimates.measure_type: % of manually coded Ebola tweets classified as alternative health information (not in line with current scientific understanding of Ebola)
estimates.value_raw: Alternative health information: 6 (2.4) of 245 (100.0) Twitter Batch 1 posts (Table 3)
estimates.denominator: 245 English-language tweets: a random ~6% subsample (299 of 4,844) of the tweets containing the keyword 'Ebola' found in a 1% random sample of the Twitter firehose (4,366,946 tweets) during the 24-hour Batch 1 window, after excluding 54 posts in languages other than English or Chinese
estimates.definition: Post coded as 'alternative health information', i.e. information that is not in line with current scientific understanding of Ebola and its prevention and control. The six Batch 1 tweets were: two on bathing in and then drinking salt water; one that the Ebola virus came from space; one that crystal meth can cure Ebola; one that Ebola arose from human cannibalism; one advising to tie a palm leaf and red cloth round head and waist and dance around a banana tree.
estimates.misinfo_def: "alternative health information (i.e., information that is not in line with current scientific understanding of Ebola and its prevention and control)"
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Manual coding and categorization of microblog contents', p. 465; Table 3, p. 471
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Posts coded by at least one coder and then recoded by the first author, who made the final decision; a second coder independently coded a random 10% of the manually coded sample. Interrater agreement with the first author was moderate for Twitter (Cohen's kappa = 0.58 for Batch 1, 0.56 for Batch 2) and substantial for Sina Weibo (0.66 and 0.78). The authors acknowledge single-coder coding as a weakness partly compensated by the 10% double-coding.
estimates.moderator_quote: We retrieved a random sample of 1% of all publicly posted tweets: (sample size: n=4,366,946 tweets from Batch 1 and n=4,305,841 tweets from Batch 2). Of these, 4,844 tweets during Batch 1 and 2,001 tweets during Batch 2 (1,109 and 465 per one million tweets, respectively) contained the keyword "Ebola".
estimates.notes: TIME SERIES COLLAPSED: the paper reports two 24-hour cross-sections a week apart; I kept Batch 1 (8-9 Aug 2014, the PHEIC-announcement window, and the larger sample) as the representative point. Batch 2 (15-16 Aug 2014) gives 2 (2.3%) of 87 — essentially identical, so the choice is immaterial. Sampling is genuinely random within a keyword corpus (unlike the popularity-truncated designs common in this literature), which is a strength; denom_selection is therefore blank rather than curated. confidence = medium because the numerator is 6 items and Twitter interrater kappa was only 0.58. Non-English tweets were not coded, which the authors flag as a limit on external validity; they also note the worst-affected West African populations relied more on offline channels, so this is not a measure of misinformation exposure in the outbreak countries. source_quote is the Table 3 row verbatim; its four columns are Twitter Batch 1, Twitter Batch 2, Sina Weibo Batch 1, Sina Weibo Batch 2, so this row's value is Twitter Batch 1 = 6 (2.4). The corresponding prose sentence in the Results is column-interleaved in the extracted PDF text and therefore not a contiguous verbatim span; it reads: 'Of 245 tweets in Batch 1 and 87 tweets in Batch 2, alternative health information ... accounted for six tweets in Batch 1 and two tweets in Batch 2.'

estimates.country: Not stated; Chinese-language posts on Sina Weibo, China's leading microblog platform (included because Twitter is blocked in China)
estimates.date: Batch 1: August 8, 2014 06:50:00 GMT to August 9, 2014 06:49:59 GMT
estimates.measure_type: % of manually coded Ebola-related Sina Weibo posts classified as alternative health information
estimates.value_raw: Alternative health information: 11 (2.4) of 452 (100.0) Sina Weibo Batch 1 posts (Table 3)
estimates.denominator: 452 Chinese-language Sina Weibo posts: a random ~6% subsample (469 of 7,645) of posts retrieved by searching the two Chinese terms for Ebola during the Batch 1 window, less 17 posts falling outside the time frame
estimates.definition: Post coded as 'alternative health information'. The eleven Batch 1 posts were: three scientific comments containing mistakes (e.g. 'from its discovery to today, Ebola had only caused havoc in West Africa'), two advocating homeopathy, and six saying traditional Chinese medicine could treat or prevent Ebola.
estimates.misinfo_def: "alternative health information (i.e., information that is not in line with current scientific understanding of Ebola and its prevention and control)"
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Manual coding and categorization of microblog contents' (Sina Weibo), p. 465; Table 3, p. 471
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same procedure as the Twitter sample: at least one coder plus final recoding by the first author, with a second coder on a random 10%; Sina Weibo interrater agreement Cohen's kappa = 0.66 (Batch 1) and 0.78 (Batch 2).
estimates.moderator_quote: Because Sina Weibo currently does not provide a streaming API service similar to that of Twitter, Chinese Ebola-related microblogs were obtained via Sina Weibo's Internet search engine. Two Chinese terms for Ebola ... were entered into the search engine. The results were then computationally captured page by page by a script.
estimates.notes: Country coded China as a judgement call: no geographic filter was applied, but the platform is China's domestic microblog, the posts are Chinese-language, and the paper's whole rationale for including Weibo is that Twitter is blocked in China. An adjudicator preferring strict literalism could recode this Global. TIME SERIES COLLAPSED to Batch 1 (larger sample, PHEIC window); Batch 2 gives 3 (1.4%) of 207. The authors argue state censorship is why rumours were rarer here and note the saltwater and Nano Silver rumours never appeared on Weibo at all — relevant to any platform comparison. Numerator is 11 items, so imprecise. Note the coded category mixes clear falsehoods (homeopathy, TCM cures) with 'scientific comments that contained mistakes', which is a looser inclusion than the Twitter examples. source_quote is the Table 3 row verbatim; its four columns are Twitter Batch 1, Twitter Batch 2, Sina Weibo Batch 1, Sina Weibo Batch 2, so this row's value is Sina Weibo Batch 1 = 11 (2.4). The corresponding prose sentence in the Results is column-interleaved in the extracted PDF text and therefore not a contiguous verbatim span; it reads: 'Of 452 posts analyzed in Batch 1 and 207 posts analyzed in Batch 2, alternative health information accounted for 11 posts in Batch 1 and three posts in Batch 2.'

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Batch 2 values not written as separate rows under the time-series collapse rule: Twitter 2 (2.3%) of 87; Sina Weibo 3 (1.4%) of 207. Both are close to their Batch 1 counterparts. 2) The abstract's summary figure ('Ebola-related misinformation constituted about 2% of Twitter and Sina Weibo content') is a rounded pooled statement; the Table 3 cell values were used instead. 3) Not extracted because they are not misinformation: 'health education and information' (Twitter 10.6%/11.5%, Weibo 12.2%/13.0%), 'responses to alternative health information' (Twitter 13.1%/11.5%, Weibo 9.5%/6.3% — these are DEBUNKING posts and must not be counted as misinformation), outbreak news, travel-ban news, the 43.0% of Batch 2 Weibo posts about the Chinese medical team, and the 6.9% of Batch 1 Weibo posts reporting the detention of a rumour-spreader. 4) Keyword and hashtag relative risks (salt RR = 0.11, water RR = 0.14, Nano Silver RR = 10.5) are frequency changes for individual terms, not shares of posts, so no row. 5) No EXPOSURE, REACH, SHARING or CONCENTRATION row is possible: the paper reports post counts and hashtag/URL shares but never the share of retweets or of views attributable to misinformation, and no user-level denominator. Table 1's shares of posts carrying a hashtag or URL are not veracity measures. 6) All other prevalence figures in the Discussion are cited from other studies and excluded under R8: 55% of Ebola tweets from Guinea/Liberia/Nigeria containing medical misinformation (Oyeyemi et al.), 54/85 (63.5%) misleading YouTube Ebola videos, 31/118 (26.3%) misleading YouTube videos, 36/100 reporting CDC transmission routes, and 'about 2% of tweets' in the 2009 influenza pandemic. 7) The tweet-level Ebola incidence rates (1,109 and 465 Ebola tweets per million tweets) quantify topic salience, not misinformation.

rob.design: Two 24-hour cross-sectional samples: Batch 1 = 8 Aug 2014 06:50 GMT to 9 Aug 06:49 GMT (immediately after the WHO PHEIC declaration), Batch 2 = the same window seven days later. Twitter: streaming API 1% random sample of the firehose (4,366,946 and 4,305,841 tweets), filtered to the keyword 'Ebola' (4,844 and 2,001 tweets); language classified in R, only English analysed. Sina Weibo: no streaming API, so a bespoke R script scraped the platform search engine for two Chinese Ebola terms every 10 minutes from two machines for redundancy; duplicates, out-of-window posts and username-only matches removed (7,377 and 3,352 posts retained). Manual coding on random subsamples drawn with an Excel RANDBETWEEN(0,100) <= 5 rule, yielding 5%-7%: Twitter 299/4,844 and 116/2,001; Weibo 469/7,645 and 207/3,416; after excluding non-English/Chinese posts and out-of-window items, 245, 87, 452 and 207 posts were coded. Coding scheme adapted from a previously published scheme, with categories including alternative health information and responses to it. Coding by at least one coder with final recoding by the first author; a second coder double-coded a random 10% — Cohen's kappa 0.58/0.56 (Twitter) and 0.66/0.78 (Weibo). Comparisons by Fisher's exact and chi-square tests. Authors' stated limits: single primary coder; only English and Chinese coded; Twitter and Weibo not representative of the global population; the worst-affected West African populations relied on offline channels, so low measured misinformation may not reflect rumours circulating there; rumours may have circulated outside the two sampling windows.
